children: By Krystal Hu

Even for someone who has spent the past decade covering this fast-moving industry, the past week felt extraordinary: researchers warning about human extinction, followed by AI lab CEOs urging a coordinated slowdown; capped by a president calling all the alarmism a hoax.

If you’re wondering how we got from hallucinating chatbots to conversations about human extinction, my colleague Aditya Soni has a useful explainer. One reason is the rapid progress in recursive self-learning, techniques that allow models to improve by training on their own outputs, which some researchers say has accelerated capabilities too fast for alignment and safety work to keep up.

Recent incidents have also made those risks feel less theoretical. Our reporting on OpenAI agents attacking Hugging Face showed how autonomous agents can operate in swarms, cover their tracks and pursue a goal while creating unintended consequences along the way.
Now, remarkably, the biggest frontier labs appear to agree on at least one thing: the pace itself may need to slow. But what would a slowdown actually look like and who has agreed to it?

This week, we take you inside Salesforce’s annual Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, where what is usually a giant marketing spectacle turned into a live debate over AI safety and control. Scroll on.

AI REGULATION? DEPENDS ON WHO YOU ASK
By
, Technology Correspondents

With the AI safety debate simmering, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff turned this year’s Dreamforce, ostensibly a giant conference about how enterprises can harness AI, into a livestreamed stage for a more consequential argument: Who decides how fast frontier AI is allowed to move?
Within hours of one another, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman took the stage in San Francisco and offered three different answers.

Speaking to roughly 10,000 people in the room and about 10 times that online, Amodei laid out the three-step plan from a 3,800-word essay he published over the weekend: Anthropic should improve its own safety practices, leading AI companies should agree on shared standards, and those standards should eventually underpin some kind of international regulatory mechanism.

“Obviously, it’s very tempting to attack your competitor and say these guys are unsafe,” said Amodei, whose company is expected to go public in weeks as we reported. A better place to start, he argued, was for companies to examine their own records, recommit to transparency and spend more on safety. Anthropic is working on that first step, he said, and plans to open a dialogue with rivals on the rest.
Then came Jensen Huang, with almost the opposite prescription.

Standing beside the 6-foot-5 Benioff, Huang joked that he wished someone would bring him a chair to stand on. But on regulation, he was unequivocal. Companies already have incentives to pace themselves until they are confident a product is safe and useful, he argued.
“We don’t need any new laws,” Huang said. The idea that the industry must choose between innovation, speed and safety, he argued, is a false one.
Hours later, Altman landed somewhere in between.

The world is right to fear AI, he said, even as he argued that the technology can be developed safely. Some accidents are inevitable with a powerful new technology, Altman said, pointing to aviation: Planes became safer not because crashes disappeared, but because incidents were investigated, reported and used to change standards.

Companies should be willing “to slow down or stop” if they reach a point where they cannot proceed safely, he said. But the aviation analogy also points to something larger than corporate judgment alone: a system of independent oversight capable of learning from failures and setting rules across an industry.
So after listening to all three, the divide seemed less about whether AI needs guardrails than about who should hold the brake.

The most tangible progress to come out of the AI safety debate has been the use of third-party evaluators with deeper access to frontier models at OpenAI and Anthropic, so external researchers can test increasingly powerful systems and provide independent checks.

But it is unclear what authority those evaluators would have to tell frontier labs, with billions on the line, that they have to go back to the drawing board and delay releasing models. That’s especially true at a time when the gap between open-source and frontier models is closing.

Washington appears unwilling to play a role here. The Trump administration’s current framework explicitly opposes creating a new federal AI rulemaking agency, while emphasizing the need to avoid unnecessary barriers to development.
“We're leading China in AI…frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump told Huang on a call on stage at the AII-In Summit this week.

Huang believes companies have commercial and legal incentives that prevent them from releasing dangerous products. Over-regulation could also stymie burgeoning U.S. open-source development. That is particularly important to Nvidia’s business because a broad ecosystem of competing model developers helps to sustain demand across its customer base while providing an alternative to powerful Chinese open-source models.

Companies also have to make business decisions — especially when trillion-dollar IPOs and enormous funding rounds are at stake. When resources are finite, do you spend them on another powerful training run or a more capable product, or do you divert some of them into expensive safety research with a commercial payoff that may be less immediate?

Recent AI-agent incidents, which my colleagues have reported on extensively, also expose a more alarming observation in this unregulated new frontier: What if the developers themselves do not fully understand what their systems are capable of?

The discovery of rogue AI activity was first uncovered by the victim, Hugging Face, and not the perpetrator, OpenAI. Outside researchers later uncovered more unreported activities. In the RubyGems case, people familiar with the matter told Reuters that OpenAI employees realized their own agents were responsible only after outside researchers identified them.

Self-regulation therefore rests on two assumptions: that companies want to restrain their systems when necessary, and that they reliably can. The recent debate suggests neither can be taken for granted — even if the companies start with the best intentions.
CHART OF THE WEEK

Americans who already use AI regularly are becoming slightly less trusting of the technology. But the real shift is among the skeptics: people who rarely or never use AI are becoming far more distrustful.

A Gallup survey released this week found that 43% of people who use AI at least sometimes said they trust it, down from 46% a year earlier. Among people who rarely or never use AI, trust fell much more sharply, to 12% from last year’s 23%.

That widening gap matters as AI companies push their products deeper into work, healthcare, education and everyday life. AI skeptics are becoming significantly harder to win over. It’s also worth noting that the survey was conducted in June, before the recent wave of rogue AI incidents and the warnings from researchers and executives about AI posing catastrophic risks.
